issues.legal_issue: A debt arising from an underlying financial transaction does not cease to be financial debt merely because the claim has been reduced to a recovery certificate, and its holder may qualify as a financial creditor entitled to initiate insolvency resolution.
material_facts: Credit facilities were advanced to borrower entities, and the corporate debtor guaranteed the facilities and mortgaged its property as security.
The creditor acquired the debt, and a compromise recorded by a court made the corporate debtor jointly and severally liable for the dues.
After default, a recovery tribunal issued recovery certificates against the borrower entities and the corporate debtor, and the certified dues remained unpaid.
The creditor applied to initiate corporate insolvency resolution against the corporate debtor.
issues.conclusion: A liability in respect of a claim arising from a recovery certificate is financial debt where it derives from an underlying financial transaction; the certificate holder is a financial creditor entitled to initiate the insolvency process.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(6), 3(10), 3(11), and 3(12) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code define claim, creditor, debt, and default broadly; Sections 5(7) and 5(8), including Section 5(8)(i), cover financial creditors and financial debt, including liability under guarantees for specified financial debts; Section 6 permits a financial creditor to initiate the process. The word “includes” ordinarily enlarges a definition, as explained in Dilworth v Commissioner of Stamps, Associated Indem Mechanical (P) Ltd. v W.B. Small Industries Development Corpn. Ltd., Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation v Ashok Iron Works Pvt. Ltd., and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v Union of India. The Code is to be read contextually and to advance its purpose of preserving the corporate debtor as a going concern while maximising recovery, as stated in Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v Union of India.

rule.if: insolvency_process_application and underlying_financial_transaction and guarantee_or_security_for_financial_debt and certified_claim_remains_unpaid

predicates.insolvency_process_application: A creditor filed an application seeking insolvency resolution against a corporate debtor.
predicates.underlying_financial_transaction: A creditor advanced money under a transaction involving consideration for the time value of money.
predicates.guarantee_or_security_for_financial_debt: The corporate debtor guaranteed or secured the underlying financial obligation.
predicates.certified_claim_remains_unpaid: A recovery tribunal issued a certificate for the debt, and some or all of the certified debt remained unpaid.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks insolvency resolution over an unpaid certified claim rooted in a financial transaction and guaranteed or secured by the corporate debtor, the certificate holder qualifies as a financial creditor entitled to initiate the process.

issues.legal_issue: Issuance of a recovery certificate for an unpaid debt gives rise to a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application, which is timely when filed within the applicable period measured from the certificate.
material_facts: The recovery certificates were issued in 2017, and the creditor filed its insolvency application in 2018.
The certified dues remained unpaid when the application was filed.
The appellate tribunal treated limitation as running from the earlier default, rather than from issuance of the recovery certificates.
issues.conclusion: The insolvency application was within limitation because it was filed within three years from issuance of the recovery certificates.
issues.legal_principle: Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to applications under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and Section 238A makes the Limitation Act applicable to proceedings under the Code. Ordinarily, limitation runs from default, but a final adjudication and recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives rise to a fresh cause of action; the application may be brought within three years from the judgment, decree, or certificate. The Court affirmed Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) v C. Shivakumar Reddy, and relied on the limitation principles in B.K. Educational Services (P) Ltd. v Parag Gupta & Associates, Jignesh Shah v Union of India, Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd., Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., and Balakrishna Savalram Pujari Waghmare v Shree Dhyaneshwar Maharaj Sansthan.

rule.if: insolvency_process_application and recovery_certificate_issued and certified_debt_remains_unpaid and application_filed_within_three_years_after_certificate

predicates.insolvency_process_application: A creditor filed an application seeking insolvency resolution against a corporate debtor.
predicates.recovery_certificate_issued: A recovery tribunal issued a certificate specifying the debt owed to the creditor.
predicates.certified_debt_remains_unpaid: Some or all of the debt specified in the certificate remained unpaid.
predicates.application_filed_within_three_years_aft: The creditor filed the insolvency application within three years after the recovery certificate was issued.

issues.definition: An insolvency application is within limitation when it concerns an unpaid certified debt and is filed within three years after issuance of the recovery certificate.

issues.legal_issue: A recovery certificate’s recognition as a decree for winding-up purposes does not restrict its use to winding-up proceedings or prevent its use to support an insolvency resolution application.
material_facts: A recovery tribunal issued certificates following adjudication of the debt.
The creditor relied on the certificates to seek insolvency resolution against the corporate debtor.
The respondents argued that the statutory treatment of the certificates as decrees applied only to winding-up proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The recovery certificates were not limited to use in winding-up proceedings and could support initiation of corporate insolvency resolution proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 19(22) and 19(22A) of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act provide for recovery certificates and deem them to be decrees or court orders for specified purposes. The Court declined to add a restriction absent from the text, applying the plain-language approach in Mohd. Shahabuddin v State of Bihar and Nasiruddin v Sita Ram Agarwal. It also considered that insolvency resolution can preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern, whereas winding-up proceedings are more severe.

predicates.insolvency_process_application: A creditor filed an application seeking insolvency resolution against a corporate debtor.
predicates.recovery_certificate_issued: A recovery tribunal issued a certificate for payment of an adjudicated debt.
predicates.certificate_deemed_court_order_for_windi: The governing law treats the recovery certificate as a court order for purposes that include winding-up proceedings.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks insolvency resolution using an issued recovery certificate that is treated as a court order for winding-up purposes, that treatment does not confine the certificate to winding-up use.

issues.legal_issue: The moratorium on suits and execution after insolvency proceedings commence does not prevent a decree-holder from initiating those proceedings when otherwise entitled to do so.
material_facts: The creditor held recovery certificates based on the adjudicated debt and applied to initiate insolvency resolution.
The respondents relied on the moratorium provision, which prohibits suits and execution against a corporate debtor after the insolvency commencement date.
issues.conclusion: The moratorium provision does not bar a decree-holder from initiating insolvency resolution; it prohibits the decree-holder from executing the decree once the process has commenced.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(a) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code prohibits institution or continuation of suits and proceedings against a corporate debtor, including execution of judgments, decrees, or orders, after the insolvency commencement date. The provision does not prevent an otherwise entitled decree-holder from applying to initiate the process; its effect is to prohibit execution during the moratorium.

predicates.insolvency_process_application: A creditor filed an application seeking insolvency resolution against a corporate debtor.
predicates.creditor_holds_decree_or_recovery_certif: The creditor holds a judgment, decree, or recovery certificate for a debt owed by the corporate debtor.

issues.definition: A creditor holding an adjudicated debt may seek insolvency resolution, even though execution of the adjudication is barred after the process commences.

issues.legal_issue: The rule that an unpaid adjudicated debt or recovery certificate can provide a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application is not per incuriam and is not inconsistent with earlier decisions addressing limitation from the original default.
material_facts: Dena Bank held that a final judgment or recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives the creditor a fresh cause of action to initiate insolvency proceedings within three years of the judgment or certificate.
The respondents argued that this holding conflicted with earlier larger-bench decisions and overlooked relevant statutory provisions.

The Court found that the earlier decisions relied on did not decide whether a judgment or recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives rise to a fresh cause of action, and that Dena Bank had considered the relevant statutory provisions.
issues.conclusion: Dena Bank correctly stated the law and was not per incuriam; its rule was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: A decision is per incuriam where it overlooks a relevant statutory provision or cannot be reconciled with an earlier decision of a co-equal or larger bench. A precedent binds for the legal principle actually decided, not for observations on issues that did not arise; the rule must be derived by applying law to the facts. The Court applied these principles from Secretary to Govt. of Kerala, Irrigation Department v James Varghese, Union of India v Dhanwanti Devi, and Regional Manager v Pawan Kumar Dubey, and distinguished Jignesh Shah and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave because neither addressed the effect of a decree or recovery certificate on limitation.

predicates.challenge_to_insolvency_precedent: A party challenging an insolvency ruling argued that the ruling was legally invalid because of earlier decisions or overlooked law.
predicates.prior_decisions_did_not_decide_certifica: The earlier decisions addressed limitation from default but did not decide whether an adjudication or recovery certificate creates a fresh limitation period.
predicates.precedent_considered_relevant_statutes: The challenged precedent considered the statutory provisions relevant to the effect of an adjudication or recovery certificate.

issues.definition: A challenged insolvency precedent remains good law when the earlier decisions did not decide the certificate’s limitation effect and the precedent considered the relevant statutory provisions.
